title: Habits live in places
hook: habits are tied to contexts, which is why holidays break routines (Wood and Neal)

segments.voice: Yesterday, cue, routine, reward: the loop, and the click at the start where a habit is easiest to see. Which loop did you spot? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-six.

A vacation. A rented room by the sea, a different bed, a different kitchen, no commute. Somewhere in there, the morning run that never gets skipped at home just quietly stops happening. So does the evening stretch, and the glass of water before bed. Nobody decided to quit. Then the suitcase comes home, the key turns in the old lock, and some of those habits switch back on almost by themselves. The other way around happens too: a habit someone has fought for years can loosen on a trip. Today's idea explains both.
screen: `A DIFFERENT BED, A DIFFERENT KITCHEN.` → `THE MORNING RUN STOPS.` → `THE KEY TURNS, IT COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the place is part of the habit. Psychologists Wendy Wood and David Neal argue that habits are tied to their contexts: the room, the time, the people around, the thing just done. The context works like yesterday's cue. Walk into the kitchen, and the kitchen starts the routine. Second, change the place and the habit can slip. In one study, Wood and her colleagues followed students who moved to a new university. Where the new setting looked like the old one, old habits like exercising or watching television tended to carry on. Where the setting changed, the habits were more likely to break, and people's intentions mattered more. A holiday is that same experiment, run on yourself. Third, this cuts both ways. A move, a new job, even rearranged furniture can be the moment a stuck habit lets go, because the old cues are gone. It can also be the moment a good habit gets lost. Fourth, the old practice of a set-aside place. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus tells his listeners, in the King James words: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." His point there is praying in secret rather than for show, not habit. But the picture he uses is a set-aside place: a closet, a door, a shut room. A cushion in one corner, a chair by one window, can work on the principle the researchers describe. Practice something often enough in one spot, and the spot itself starts helping. The place holds it.
screen: `THE PLACE IS PART OF THE HABIT.` · `A NEW CAMPUS, OLD HABITS SLIP.` · `IT CUTS BOTH WAYS.` · then, large: `ENTER INTO THY CLOSET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick a place. Look around where you are right now. Is this a spot you could come back to tomorrow, and the day after? A particular chair, a corner of the bed, a step on the back porch. If it is, sit here on purpose, and feel the details: the light, the sounds, what's under you. If it isn't, picture the place that could be, and sit with that picture. Either way, you're choosing a spot the practice can live in. Rest on the breath, and let the place soak in. The bell holds the time.
Habits live in places. A habit is tied to its setting, so a new place can break it, and a chosen place can hold it. Today's word.

Your line: the place holds it. Today, go back to the spot you picked, even for one minute, and do one breath of practice there. Start teaching the place what it's for. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Some people who keep a daily practice set aside one place for it, a corner, a chair, a cushion, a prayer space, and return there each day, so the setting itself becomes part of the habit.

fork.setup: you've moved to a new apartment and want to keep a daily practice going. what do you do first?
options: rely on willpower until it sticks again.
choose one spot in the new place and practice there every day.
wait until the new place feels like home.
fork.reveal: habits live in places. a chosen spot gives the practice a new context to attach to.

trapdoor: what you thought: a habit lives inside a person, like a trait.
what it means: a habit is tied to its setting, the room, the time, what you just did.
what a scholar hears: Wood and Neal treat context as the cue itself, which is why moving house can both break and free a habit, and why intentions matter more in new settings.

notes: Confirm the description of Wood, Tam and Witt: students transferring universities; habits (exercising, reading the paper, watching TV) persisted when the new context was similar and were more likely to be disrupted, with intentions guiding behavior more, when it differed.
'Some spiritual traditions noticed something like this too' is a general statement; the script then names one sourced example (Matthew 6:6). A reviewer may prefer to cut the general sentence.
The vacation scene is illustrative, not a research finding.
Matthew 6:6 is cited as one tradition's text, not as an instruction to the listener; confirm KJV wording.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced 'some spiritual traditions noticed something like this' and added that Matthew 6:6 is about praying in secret rather than for show, so the verse isn't presented as a teaching about habit.
